Utilization is printed on every screen because it is the number that finds a thrashing locus. It is on no invoice, because a carrier can sit at full utilization and admit nothing — charging for it would be charging the customer for our own placement decisions.
Every figure anywhere on this surface is a placeholder.

The measured production floor is a few hundred cycles per transition, so a million transitions is a fraction of a second of one core. A price is not derivable from that until a kernel counts admitted transitions under load, and until then no number on the site may be presented as a rate anyone could pay.

Not ruled. A design constraint on the meter that gate 1 in §4 will build, recorded here because the record shape is a one-way door: once evidentiary counts exist, reshaping them means rewriting receipts, and this tree does not rewrite receipts.
A transition records a class, not a cost.
The meter writes a small class symbol per admitted transition — countable by a kernel taught nothing about cycles — and the cost lives in one calibrated
, recorded once per group. An invoice is
Three things follow, and they are why the shape is fixed before the kernel exists:
The counter ships before the price.
The counts are evidentiary and arrive with gate 1; the

scale is a separately versioned artifact that arrives with gate 4. The absence of a price is then visible in the data — there is no scale row — rather than maintained by a launch gate refusing to print one. §2's prohibition stops being a promise and becomes a missing column.
A repricing does not rewrite evidence.
Re-pricing a past period reissues one versioned scale
against immutable counts. Per-event pricing would make the same correction a rewrite of every record in the period.
The record stops outgrowing the work.
Per-event storage is O(transitions); this is

O(classes × epochs), flat in volume. At §2's floor of a few hundred cycles per transition a per-event record is larger than the work it describes: a saturated core at a 0.1 % duty cycle produces on the order of 10^10 transitions a month, and a 32-byte record each makes the billing data cost more than the compute it bills. This is not a performance argument — the meter is not on a hot enough path for that to matter. It is that the naive record is inverted.
Group by transition class and epoch. Never by carrier occupancy, and never across tenants.
A scale shared between loci makes one customer's invoice move when another's loci behave differently, and

puts more loci than slots on a carrier by design — so a carrier-scoped scale spans customers. That is §2's utilization ban in a new outfit: the same coupling, the same objection, harder to see. Volume pricing is where someone will reach for it.
Expensive classes get their own group.

A group's scale is dominated by its largest member. A rehome, a large state migration or a cold seal re-establishment averaged in with a few-hundred-cycle ordinary transition either overbills every ordinary transition in the group or eats the outlier. Ternary weight quantization, where this representation comes from, spreads outliers by rotating the basis before rounding; a bill cannot be rotated, so the only answer left is to keep those classes in groups of their own, or on their own invoice line.
2b) Settlement — how a customer pays, and what paying does not buy
Three clauses RULED 2026-09-19 — R89, R90, R91 in the root `REVISION_REGISTER.md`. The mechanism is unwritten and nothing is built.

They were ruled ahead of the mechanism for §2a's own reason: the shape is a one-way door. Once a balance has moved between two parties it cannot be made non-transferable afterwards, and once admission consults a payment rail the floor's latency claim is a claim about somebody else's ledger. The full contract, its ten refusals and their controls are
; this section is what it means for this surface.
What is sold is what §2a counts: admitted transitions of a class.
A purchase credits a balance denominated in the versioned

— not in dollars, not in requests, not in machine-hours. So settlement inherits §2a whole: counts stay immutable, a repricing still reissues one scale row against them, and the absence of a price is still a missing scale row rather than a promise.
The rail is x402, and we are the seller — never an issuer.

, settled in stablecoins by the payer's own facilitator. It requires us to mint no instrument, run no chain and hold no float beyond an unspent balance. It is also the shape an agent can use without a human in the loop, which is the only shape that matches a locus that runs while nobody is watching.
A coin was considered and is not the direction
; the five gates below are what a coin would have to clear, and none of them is cleared.
The invariant, which is `custody-model.md`'s with one word changed:
Paying for something cannot grant lifecycle authority over it.
. Four consequences, each of which is a refusal this surface is bound by:
An exhausted balance never ends a live locus.
locus is a lifecycle event needing a lineage decision and a receipt, exactly like a suspend. If a payment rail can end a locus, payment has become authority.
A balance never moves between accounts — R89.
It may be funded by a third party, spent across

many loci under one account, and refunded to the method that funded it. It may never be sold, gifted, split out or assigned. That is the line between a credit and an instrument, and it is what makes "seller, never issuer" true by construction rather than by assertion.
The floor never consults a budget — R90.
An unfunded request refuses at ingress, before the
floor. Admission may depend on a payment profile's
. This is forced by the invariant above: if an exhausted balance may never end a live locus, there was nothing the floor needed a budget for.
Charging per call is charging for
utilization ban in an HTTP header.
No balance is per-carrier and none is shared across tenants.
puts more loci than slots on a carrier; a balance is the same object one step later.
A settlement that fails after work was admitted is a **debt event
appended to the lineage**, never a retraction of a count. This tree does not rewrite receipts.
`computedriven` owns the count format; locu.systems owns the money — R91.
Settlement gets no crate in the substrate: a substrate carrying our billing model cannot be run by anyone who is not us. What remains there is a negative constraint,
Settlement is a fourth clause, beside the three the fabric already states
— discovery chooses where we try, authentication decides whom we reached, only the lineage decides what they may do — and it adds:
settlement decides how much may be spent; never whom, never what, never where.
§6 still stands in full. Accepting a payment rail is not a plan anyone can buy: there is no price (gate 4), nothing to spend a balance on (gate 1), and nobody to sell to (gate 5).

Compute was local in R4's picture. Locus hosting rents machines to run somebody else's compute, was ruled a month later, and inherited a provider list by assumption. The reasoning is

So the carriers this surface may name are:
— the stable plane. Long-lived carriers, and the database and control plane beside them
— burst carriers, placed and destroyed by code. Per-second billing, and
single-attach volumes that hold locus state when the carrier under it goes
— a T&R box in their own building is a carrier like any other, and on that
arrangement the carrier bill never reaches our invoice
Cloudflare is not a carrier and cannot become one.
It keeps Pages, Workers and R2. A carrier has to give us a kernel we boot — the confinement floor installs its own Landlock ruleset (ABI 9, measured on kernel 7.2.2) and seccomp allow-list, and
, whose private half lives in the kernel's own WireGuard implementation. Workers and Containers give none of that, and cap an instance at ½ vCPU. This is a capability fact, not a preference.
A carrier must also expose a provisioning API.

Gate 2 in §4 is an adapter that places a locus and returns what happened; an adapter cannot be written against a host that is provisioned by filling in a web form. That requirement is what removes KnownHost and HostGator, and HostGator separately forbids the workload — its "unmetered" bandwidth is defined as not exceeding 25 % of system resources for longer than 90 seconds, and a carrier holding loci runs continuously.
